title: Advertising techniques
examples: How do advertisers try to make us buy things?
Who is an advertisement usually trying to talk to?

explain.say: Today we are looking at how adverts try to convince you.

items: Adverts try to convince you to do something.
They use techniques to change your mind.

explain.say: Persuasion means trying to convince someone to agree.
One way adverts persuade is by showing emotion.
Another technique is appealing to your sense of belonging.
The target audience is who the advert is meant for.
For example, a cereal advert for young children uses bright colours.

faq.q: What is the difference between persuasion and just telling me something?
faq.a: Persuasion is when the advert tries to change your feelings or actions. It uses feelings to make you want something.
asks: How is persuasion different from information?

faq.q: Why do advertisers care about the target audience?
faq.a: They need to know who they are talking to so the advert makes sense to that group. A message for kids is different from one for adults.
asks: Should I always know the target audience?

faq.q: Can an advert use fear to persuade me?
faq.a: Yes, sometimes adverts use fear to make you think you need their product. They might show what could go wrong without it.
asks: Is using fear in ads okay?

faq.q: What does it mean if an advert targets teenagers?
faq.a: It means the advert is designed using things that teenagers care about. This might be friendship or looking cool.
Not always. Sometimes the emotion is used just to distract you from looking at the facts. You should always look closely.
asks: How do I spot fake emotion?

facts: Persuasion is the act of convincing someone to believe or do something.
The target audience helps advertisers choose the right style and message.
Advertisers often use emotion, like happiness or fear, to connect with people.
A message for young children will look very different from one for adults.

quiz.say: If an advert for video games only shows fast-paced action and bright lights, it is likely targeting:
quiz.why: Fast action and bright lights appeal strongly to the interests and attention of teenagers.

wrong.0: Seniors often prefer calmer, more informational, or nostalgic advertising styles.
wrong.1: Family adverts usually try to balance action with moments of calm connection.
wrong.3: Young children often prefer simpler, more colourful, and less intense visuals.

quiz.say: An advert for sunscreen shows a dramatic storm cloud over a beach, followed by bright sunshine with people swimming. This combination of visuals is an example of:
quiz.why: The advert contrasts the bad thing (storm) with the good thing (sunshine) to make the product seem necessary.

wrong.1: The focus is on the weather contrast, not just fitting in with other people.
wrong.2: While emotion is used, the method of persuasion here is setting up a contrast between two states.
wrong.3: This describes the technique, not the group the advert is aimed at.
